To model the clustering of diffuse ionized gas into the non-linear regime without introducing many nuisance parameters, the authors build a Hybrid Effective Field Theory (HEFT) model that uses the full gravitational displacement field from a dark-matter-only $N$-body simulation and adds just two effective parameters: a Lorentzian feedback suppression scale $c_f^2$ (treating feedback as a small-scale pseudo-pressure) and a single linear Lagrangian bias $b_{1,d}^L$ (justified because $\sim 95\%$ of baryons remain diffuse, suppressing higher-order bias terms from stars and neutral gas). They validate this prescription against nine hydrodynamical feedback variants in the FLAMINGO simulation suite and compare it to a full second-order HEFT expansion, confirming that higher-order Lagrangian bias terms and stochasticity are negligible. By achieving percent-level accuracy down to $k \sim 1$–$1.5\,h/\mathrm{Mpc}$ with only two parameters, the model provides a compact way to constrain baryonic feedback with FRB DM and kSZ observations and inform weak-lensing cosmology.

papers.title: Interpretable morphology-based marked statistics
papers.authors: Federico Semenzato, Benjamin D. Wandelt, Michele Liguori, Alvise Raccanelli
papers.abstract: The shapes and environments of cosmic structures carry cosmological information beyond the matter power spectrum. Recovering this information while retaining a physical understanding is a central challenge for cosmological inference. We construct an interpretable, rotation-equivariant neural marking scheme that reweights the matter field, combining learned density responses with explicit measures of local morphology. This approach enables direct inspection of the learned transformations, while retaining the advantages of a two-point function analysis. We employ a contrastive learning framework to align the marked summaries with the respective cosmological parameters. In real-space matter simulations, the learned marked spectra recover information beyond the ordinary power spectrum, tightening marginalized Fisher constraints on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_m$ by factors of $1.7\times$ and $1.5\times$ relative to the power spectrum plus bispectrum at $k_{\mathrm{max}}=0.3\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. Without retraining, our mark also improves a neutrino-mass forecast by a factor of $1.5\times$ relative to the power spectrum at the same scale cut. Across the cosmological prior, our marking scheme also improve the prediction errors in both parameters by $1.3\times$ over the best tested classical mark at $k_{\mathrm{max}}=0.2\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. A qualitative comparison with neural forecasts motivates the possibility that these different compressions approach a common information level. Neural marked statistics thus offer a route to extracting non-Gaussian information from cosmological surveys, combining interpretable, physically motivated transformations with the practical advantages of two-point estimators.

conclusions: In Fisher forecasts on $z=0$ Quijote matter simulations at $k_{\mathrm{max}}=0.2\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, the soft-gated Hessian Mark tightens marginalized constraints on $\sigma_8$ by $6.5\times$ and $\Omega_m$ by $3.0\times$ relative to the standard matter power spectrum.

At $k_{\mathrm{max}}=0.3\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, the Hessian Mark outperforms the joint power spectrum plus bispectrum by factors of $1.7\times$ on $\sigma_8$ and $1.5\times$ on $\Omega_m$, and without any retraining improves a neutrino-mass forecast by $1.5\times$ over the power spectrum alone.

Across the full cosmological prior, neural parameter regression using the Hessian Mark reduces prediction RMSE on $\Omega_m$ and $\sigma_8$ by $1.3\times$ compared to the best tested classical density-only mark at $k_{\mathrm{max}}=0.2\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$.

Ablation tests show that while global box-to-box variations in the environment-gate mixture drive most of the $\sigma_8$ gain, the spatial morphology pattern itself is essential for tightening $\Omega_m$ and $n_s$ constraints (removing it degrades their gains by $15\text{--}17\%$ and $23\text{--}28\%$).

ai.summary: Nonlinear gravitational collapse turns initially Gaussian density fluctuations into a rich cosmic web of voids, sheets, filaments, and clusters, pushing cosmological information out of the standard two-point power spectrum and into harder-to-model higher-order statistics. In this paper, the authors design an interpretable, rotation-equivariant neural marking scheme—most notably a "Hessian Mark"—that combines a learned radial density filter with four density-response "experts" softly gated by the eigenvalues of the log-density Hessian (which measure local cosmic-web curvature), trained via contrastive learning on Quijote $N$-body simulations to extract information complementary to the unmarked power spectrum. Because every ingredient (filter, curvature gates, and density responses) remains explicit, the method recovers substantial non-Gaussian information—outperforming both classical density marks and the power spectrum plus bispectrum—while letting cosmologists directly inspect which physical environments drive the improved constraints.

papers.title: Four consistent estimates of $H_0$ from a $Λ$CDM inference network given CMB data
papers.authors: Gabriel P. Lynch, Lloyd Knox
papers.abstract: We organize inferences from cosmic microwave background (CMB) data, of the current rate of expansion, $H_0$, into a network whose structure is informed by a scaling symmetry of the Einstein-Boltzmann evolution equations. There are four distinct routes through this network from a calibrating anchor to $H_0$. Given key assumptions of the $\Lambda$CDM model, they are mutually consistent. This consistency is a significant feature of the $\Lambda$CDM model's compatibility with CMB data. The redundancy in $H_0$ determinations illuminates a hurdle to resolving the $H_0$ tension with alternative cosmological models.

conclusions: The four CMB routes to $H_0$ are mutually consistent ($\chi^2 = 3.47$ for 3 degrees of freedom, $\mathrm{PTE} = 0.32$): Radiation gives $67.20 \pm 0.57$, Pressure support $66.7 \pm 1.6$, Free streaming $68.3 \pm 2.7$, and Thomson scattering $65.7 \pm 1.2\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ (combined $\Lambda$CDM: $67.78 \pm 0.42$).

Isolating the information from the three non-standard routes yields an estimate uncorrelated with the usual radiation/sound-horizon route of $H_0 = 68.44 \pm 0.63\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$—nearly the same precision and consistent within $1.5\sigma$.

Using only the gravitational signature of pressure-supported matter in the CMB, the authors obtain a $3\%$ constraint on the baryon fraction, $f_{\rm ps} = 0.1580 \pm 0.0047$, which agrees with independent DESI DR1 galaxy clustering measurements ($0.161 \pm 0.010$).

Replacing the CMB-inferred $\Omega_m$ with uncalibrated DESI DR2 BAO raises all four $H_0$ values by $3\%$ (e.g., to $69.3 \pm 1.1$ for the radiation route), still well below the Local Distance Network value ($73.50 \pm 0.81\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$).

Because four physically distinct routes agree on a low $H_0$, resolving the Hubble tension with new physics requires either breaking all four $\Lambda$CDM assumptions in lockstep (e.g., via a mirror dark sector plus fine-tuned helium abundance) or biasing multiple invariants consistently; keeping the pressure-support assumption $\omega_{ps}=\omega_b$ also explains why early-universe solutions tend to push $\omega_b$ above BBN bounds.

ai.summary: The Hubble tension—the $>6\sigma$ discrepancy between local distance-ladder measurements of $H_0$ and the value inferred from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) under $\Lambda$CDM—has proven remarkably resistant to theoretical fixes. Exploiting a scaling symmetry of the linearized Einstein–Boltzmann equations (where rescaling all gravitational free-fall rates, interaction rates, and wavenumbers leaves the CMB power spectra unchanged), Lynch and Knox show that CMB spectra alone only constrain six dimensionless ratios ("invariants"), while the absolute scale of $H_0$ enters only through the FIRAS CMB temperature measurement. They organize $\Lambda$CDM's inference of $H_0$ into a network with four distinct physical routes from FIRAS to $H_0$, each relying on a single modeling assumption (standard total radiation, pressure-supported matter being baryons, free-streaming radiation being neutrinos, or the standard Thomson scattering rate) before sharing a final late-time step via $\Omega_m$. Using primary CMB data from Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 (and cross-checking with DESI BAO and galaxy clustering), they relax three assumptions at a time and find that all four routes yield mutually consistent, low values of $H_0$. This redundancy is a strong internal consistency test passed by $\Lambda$CDM and clarifies why alternative cosmological models struggle to raise $H_0$ without finely tuned or BBN-conflicting modifications.

papers.title: The Simons Observatory: Analysis of methods for polarization calibration of multiple instruments
papers.authors: The Simons Observatory Collaboration : Anto I. Lonappan, Patricia Diego-Palazuelos, Carlos Hervías-Caimapo, Kam Arnold, Susanna Azzoni, Carlo Baccigalupi, Matteo Billi, Erminia Calabrese, Yuji Chinone, Matthew Chu, Mark Devlin, Josquin Errard, Nicholas Galitzki, Bradley R. Johnson, Brian Keating, Andréa Landais, Toshiya Namikawa, Federico Nati, Giuseppe Puglisi, Christian L. Reichardt, Kevin Wolz
papers.abstract: Cosmic birefringence, the rotation of the CMB linear polarization plane across the Universe, is a powerful test of parity-violating physics beyond the Standard Model. Static isotropic rotation, however, is limited by an instrument's absolute polarization-angle calibration. We present a method for transferring absolute calibration between Simons Observatory (SO) instruments, validated on map-level simulations of the Large Aperture Telescope (LAT) and Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) with lensed CMB polarization, polarized Galactic foregrounds, correlated instrumental noise, and polarization-angle miscalibration. We develop two pipelines: a joint LAT+SAT likelihood transferring calibration through their overlap, and the Minami-Komatsu foreground-based method, which separates cosmic birefringence from instrumental miscalibration using Galactic dust polarization without an external angle prior. We derive a general variance budget showing that calibration transfer improves sensitivity only when the combined reference and overlap transfer uncertainties remain below the receiving instrument's calibration uncertainty. While transfer does not lower the absolute-angle floor for isotropic $\beta$, it anchors the receiving instrument's multipole range. The relative-angle uncertainty is $\sim 0.1^\circ$ for $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=300$, improving to $\sim 0.04^\circ$ at $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}=600$, subject to SAT beam and transfer-function control. Finally, for $\beta=0.3^\circ$, we show how the LAT's $\ell$-range distinguishes scale-independent dark-energy rotation from scale-dependent axion dark-matter models via $C_\ell^{EB}$.

conclusions: Transferring absolute polarization-angle calibration between telescopes only improves sensitivity when the reference uncertainty combined in quadrature with the overlap relative-angle uncertainty $\sigma(\Delta\alpha)$ is smaller than the receiving instrument's own calibration uncertainty; when the SAT is better calibrated, combined constraints reach $\sigma(\beta) \simeq 0.04^\circ$–$0.02^\circ$, though transfer cannot beat the reference instrument's absolute-angle floor.

In the baseline setup, the transferred LAT measurement is bottlenecked by the LAT–SAT relative-angle uncertainty ($\sigma(\Delta\alpha) \sim 0.1^\circ$ for $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}} = 300$), which improves by a factor of $\sim 3$ to $\sim 0.04^\circ$ if $\ell_{\max}^{\mathrm{SAT}}$ is pushed to $600$—yielding a bigger gain than moving from Baseline to Goal noise ($\sigma(\beta_{\rm LAT})$ from $0.09^\circ$ to $0.06^\circ$).

The Minami–Komatsu foreground-based estimator provides an unbiased, systematics-independent cross-check, recovering an ensemble mean $\beta = 0.298^\circ \pm 0.004^\circ$ (with $0.041^\circ$ per-realization scatter) for a fiducial $\beta = 0.3^\circ$ across 100 simulations, contingent on the assumed Galactic dust $EB$ model.

For a fiducial $\beta = 0.3^\circ$, the LAT's wide multipole coverage can distinguish a scale-independent dark-energy-like rotation from oscillatory axion dark-matter $C_\ell^{EB}$ templates across $m_\phi \in [0.7, 6.4] \times 10^{-28}\,\mathrm{eV}$, whereas the SAT alone has weaker shape discrimination at lower masses.
ai.summary: Cosmic birefringence is a uniform rotation of the cosmic microwave background's (CMB) linear polarization plane as photons travel across the Universe, which would signal parity-violating new physics (such as a dark-energy-like or axion dark-matter pseudoscalar field coupled to photons) by mixing parity-even $E$ modes into parity-odd $B$ modes to create a non-zero $C_\ell^{EB}$ spectrum. Measuring an isotropic rotation angle $\beta$ is fundamentally limited by how well a telescope's absolute polarization angle is calibrated, since a global instrumental miscalibration mimics the exact same signal. Using 100 map-level simulations of the Simons Observatory's Large Aperture Telescope (LAT) and Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) with lensed CMB, Galactic foregrounds, and correlated noise, the authors develop and validate two complementary pipelines: a joint LAT+SAT likelihood that transfers angle calibration between instruments through their shared sky overlap, and the Minami–Komatsu method, which uses Galactic dust polarization to separate cosmic rotation from instrumental miscalibration without an external angle prior. They derive a general variance budget showing exactly when cross-instrument calibration transfer improves sensitivity, and demonstrate how the LAT's high-multipole reach can distinguish a constant dark-energy-like rotation from a scale-dependent axion dark-matter signal.

papers.title: Primordial black holes production in Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity
papers.authors: Ekaterina O. Pozdeeva, Sergey Yu. Vernov
papers.abstract: We consider models with the Gauss-Bonnet term multiplied to a function of the scalar field and propose a new inflationary model which provides a mechanism for the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). For certain values of the model parameters, the predictions of this model agree with observational data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT). Due to estimation of possiable PBHs masses, we demonstrate that they can be considered as a possible source for all or part of dark matter.

conclusions: The proposed model agrees with recent ACT/DESI and Planck/BICEP constraints, predicting a scalar spectral index $n_s = 0.974$, a tensor-to-scalar ratio $r = 0.0146$ (well below the $r < 0.028$ limit), and a scalar amplitude $\mathcal{P}_\zeta \approx 2.10 \times 10^{-9}$.

Numerical integration of the full dynamical system shows that the squared propagation speeds of both scalar ($c_s^2$) and tensor ($c_t^2$) perturbations stay positive throughout inflation, confirming the model avoids gradient instabilities.

The Gauss-Bonnet-induced ultra-slow-roll phase boosts the scalar power spectrum by more than 6 orders of magnitude, yielding PBH masses between $1.68 \times 10^{-17}\,M_\odot$ and $4.10 \times 10^{-12}\,M_\odot$ (asteroid-mass black holes that remain viable dark matter candidates).

Varying the PBH mass and total inflationary duration ($N_{\text{tot}} \approx 59\text{--}66$ e-folds) requires heavy fine-tuning of the coupling parameter $\xi_0$ (at the level of $10^{-5}\text{--}10^{-6}$), a common issue in single-field ultra-slow-roll PBH scenarios.
ai.summary: Primordial black holes (PBHs)—hypothetical black holes formed from extreme density fluctuations in the early Universe rather than collapsing stars—are a viable dark matter candidate, and producing them in single-field inflation typically requires a brief "ultra-slow-roll" (USR) phase where the inflaton field stalls to amplify small-scale perturbations. However, a USR phase usually lowers the scalar spectral index $n_s$, creating tension between existing Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet (EGB) inflationary models (which add a string-inspired, higher-order curvature term coupled to the inflaton) and recent Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) and DESI measurements ($n_s = 0.9743 \pm 0.0034$). Pozdeeva and Vernov construct a new single-field EGB model with an exponential potential and a localized Gauss-Bonnet coupling $\xi(\phi)$, then numerically integrate the exact background evolution equations to track the full inflationary trajectory. Without the Gauss-Bonnet term, their potential ends inflation too early, but the localized coupling simultaneously extends inflation to ~60 e-folds, triggers the USR phase needed for PBH formation, and preserves agreement with ACT/DESI observations.

papers.title: Higgs-portal dark matter beyond kinetic equilibrium
papers.authors: Giorgio Arcadi, Michele Benaco, Mattia Di Mauro, Sami Nurmi, Kimmo Tuominen
papers.abstract: We revisit the scalar, vector, and fermion Higgs-portal dark matter models in the resonant regime without assuming kinetic equilibrium during the freeze-out. We compute the relic abundance by solving the full momentum-dependent Boltzmann equation and compare the results with the standard momentum-averaged treatment. We find that the standard treatment significantly underestimates the relic abundance below the resonance, apart from the fermionic case with a purely scalar portal coupling where the difference is negligible. The deviation from the standard treatment is largest for fermionic models with pseudoscalar interactions, corresponding to factor of 10 in terms of the coupling that reproduces the correct relic abundance. For the scalar and vector cases the corresponding difference is up to a factor of 2. We confront the resulting parameter space with the latest constraints from direct and indirect detection, as well as collider experiments. We find the full momentum-dependent results systematically strengthen the direct detection constraints.

conclusions: Below the Higgs resonance ($m_{\rm DM} < m_h/2$), the standard kinetic-equilibrium approximation consistently underestimates the DM relic density (by up to ~80% at fixed coupling in the pseudoscalar fermion case) because resonant annihilation depletes high-momentum DM particles faster than elastic scattering can replenish them.

To match the observed relic abundance ($\Omega_{\rm DM}h^2 = 0.120$), scalar and vector DM require portal couplings up to a factor of 2 larger than the standard calculation predicts, while Dirac fermions with purely pseudoscalar (CP-violating) couplings require couplings up to a factor of 10 larger.

For fermionic DM with a purely scalar (CP-conserving) coupling, annihilation is $p$-wave suppressed, which forces larger couplings that keep DM in kinetic equilibrium; here the full treatment matches the standard result, and the model is already ruled out by LZ direct-detection limits.

Because larger couplings are needed to avoid overproducing DM, the full momentum-dependent treatment systematically tightens direct-detection (LZ, future DARWIN) and invisible Higgs decay (ATLAS) bounds—leaving future xenon detectors able to exclude most of the remaining scalar and vector parameter space, while pseudoscalar fermions remain mainly testable via invisible Higgs decays and gamma-ray searches.
ai.summary: In "Higgs-portal" models—some of the simplest particle-physics candidates for dark matter (DM)—the dark sector communicates with the Standard Model solely through the Higgs boson, and the main surviving parameter space lies near the resonance $m_{\rm DM} \simeq m_h/2$, where DM pairs can annihilate efficiently through an almost on-shell Higgs with very small couplings. Standard thermal freeze-out calculations assume kinetic equilibrium (that elastic scattering with the primordial plasma keeps DM in a thermal momentum distribution), but near a narrow resonance, annihilations selectively deplete high-momentum DM particles faster than weak elastic scattering can replenish them. Using the numerical code DRAKE, the authors solve the full momentum-dependent Boltzmann equation across scalar, vector, and Dirac-fermion Higgs-portal models, and confront the updated relic-density predictions with current and projected constraints from direct detection (LZ, DARWIN), gamma-ray indirect detection (Fermi-LAT), and invisible Higgs decays (ATLAS). They show that accounting for early kinetic decoupling significantly shifts the couplings needed to reproduce the observed DM abundance ($\Omega_{\rm DM}h^2 = 0.120$) below the resonance, which in turn tightens experimental bounds on these minimal DM scenarios.

papers.title: Refined, Reliable and Reproducible: Algorithmic Analysis and Reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder
papers.authors: Alvaro Roy Schachner, Dante Javier Paz, Juan Antonio Rico Gallego, Carlos Mauricio Correa, Andrés Nicolás Ruiz, Sebastián Rogelio Gualpa, Juan Bautista Cabral
papers.abstract: Cosmic voids are vast underdense regions of the Universe that encode valuable information about its large-scale structure and evolution. By extending spherical voids into overlapping sphere structures, the Popcorn Void Finder demonstrated an improved statistical characterization of cosmic void populations. However, its origin as a research prototype progressively hindered its maintainability and extensibility. Moreover, post-publication algorithmic modifications have not been systematically evaluated, leaving their statistical and computational consequences insufficiently characterized. In this work, we present a comprehensive reimplementation of the Popcorn Void Finder, prioritizing algorithmic transparency, maintainability, and reproducibility. We document the complete identification procedure, revisit the original algorithmic choices, and evaluate their statistical and computational consequences. Comparisons between implementations revealed a significant change in the behavior of the Void Size Function, which is now characterized by a power-law regime transitioning to a Schechter-like distribution. These changes not only provide a better characterization of void sizes, but enable a new and more robust method to the determination of the shot-noise dominated regime, without implicit dependencies on internal finder parameters present in previous works. Performance benchmarks demonstrate a 1.62x speedup in spherical void identification and a substantial improvement in overlap-removal throughput. We determined the Popcorn algorithm to be negatively affected by load imbalance, and found a speedup of 63x in a tested configuration with a newly introduced early growth termination criterion. These results establish a more maintainable and reproducible foundation for popcorn void identification, while clarifying the statistical and computational trade-offs that govern its performance.

conclusions: **Cleaner Void Size Function & shot-noise scale:** Replacing the original random-walk recentering with an in-cell recentering strategy yields a Void Size Function (VSF) that follows a clean power law at small scales transitioning to a Schechter-like distribution at large radii, allowing the shot-noise-dominated regime to be identified robustly without hidden dependencies on internal finder parameters.

**Major computational speedups:** Benchmarks show a $1.62\times$ speedup for spherical void identification and much higher overlap-removal throughput; furthermore, because popcorn growth suffers from parallel load imbalance, introducing an adaptive early growth termination criterion yields a $62.9\times$ speedup in a tested configuration with only a small loss in statistical quality.

**Reproducibility and usability:** The rewritten C++ codebase (OpenMP/MPI, optional HDF5) reduces code size and complexity, enforces deterministic scheduling with explicit random seeds, remains backward-compatible with legacy files, and ships with a new Python API (`pvfpy`) supporting visualization, VSF analysis, and prolate-ellipsoid void representations.
ai.relevance_reason: Cosmic voids are a standard large-scale structure probe of dark energy and modified gravity, so a faster, reproducible void finder is useful background tooling for simulation analysis, though this paper is primarily a software-engineering and algorithmic reimplementation rather than beyond-$\Lambda$CDM modelling or inhomogeneous cosmology.
ai.summary: Cosmic voids—vast underdense regions of the cosmic web—are powerful probes of dark energy and modified gravity because they are less affected by complex baryonic physics than dense galaxy clusters. While simple spherical void finders often fragment irregularly shaped underdense regions, the Popcorn Void Finder (PVF) generalizes them by iteratively growing unions of overlapping spheres from spherical seeds while maintaining an integrated density contrast threshold $\Delta_v$. Because the original PVF was an undocumented research prototype, the authors present a complete, transparent C++ reimplementation (with OpenMP/MPI parallelization and a companion Python API, `pvfpy`), systematically documenting every algorithmic stage and benchmarking its statistical and computational trade-offs. Beyond making the code deterministic and maintainable, their algorithmic refinements—including an in-cell recentering scheme and an adaptive early growth termination criterion—dramatically accelerate void identification and yield a more regular, parameter-independent characterization of small-scale void abundances.

papers.title: Finite-Temperature Stabilization of a KKLT Modulus in Three-Dimensional Lattice Simulations
papers.authors: Saya Mahmoudi, Furkan Utku Biber, Hyukjung Kim, Heeseung Zoe
papers.abstract: We investigate the cosmological stabilization of a KKLT modulus through three-dimensional Langevin lattice simulations incorporating an evolving thermal bath, dissipation, spatial gradients, and stochastic fluctuations. While the spatially averaged modulus closely follows homogeneous evolution away from the capture threshold, near-critical trajectories linger near the unstable potential barrier for approximately one e-fold, allowing long-wavelength fluctuations to undergo tachyonic amplification and drive localized regions across the barrier even as the mean field turns back toward the stabilized vacuum. Linear Langevin theory reproduces the fluctuation growth, while convergence tests identify a narrow stochastic layer in which the barrier-crossing fraction shows no systematic dependence on the discretization at a fixed effective distance from the threshold. These results demonstrate that capture of the spatially averaged modulus does not guarantee that every spatial region remains within the stabilizing barrier.

conclusions: **Homogeneous capture does not guarantee local stabilization:** Within a narrow stochastic layer of width $\gamma - \gamma_{\rm c} \sim (3\text{--}6)\times 10^{-4}$ above the homogeneous capture threshold ($\gamma_{\rm c} = 0.499529$ in the reference model), lingering near the barrier top for $\sim 1$ e-fold triggers tachyonic growth that drives localized spatial regions over the barrier even as the mean field turns back toward the minimum.

**Linear Langevin theory matches the lattice:** Analytical linear Langevin predictions reproduce the Hubble-smoothed fluctuation amplitude to within $\sim 5\text{--}10\%$ and match the lattice barrier-crossing plateau with a ratio of $0.96 \pm 0.13$ (and an estimated stochastic layer width of $5\times 10^{-4}$).

**Cutoff-insensitive observables:** Unlike the raw lattice variance, which is dominated by UV grid modes, the Hubble-smoothed variance $\sigma_H$ and crossing fraction $f_{\rm cross}^H$ are stable across resolutions and show no systematic discretization dependence when compared at a fixed effective distance from the capture threshold.

**Open fate and model dependence:** Extended simulations show some barrier-crossed regions continuing toward larger field values, though determining whether they truly decompactify requires inhomogeneous gravitational dynamics; the exact threshold also shifts with the thermal coupling $r$, friction law, and the compressed KKLT hierarchy ($a\sigma_{\min}=4$) used for numerical feasibility.
ai.summary: In string theory, compactifying extra dimensions produces scalar fields called *moduli* that control the size of those dimensions; in the standard KKLT (Kachru–Kallosh–Linde–Trivedi) scenario, the volume modulus sits in a metastable minimum separated from runaway decompactification by a potential barrier. In the hot early universe, a rolling modulus can easily overshoot this barrier unless Hubble expansion or thermal friction slows it down, and finite-temperature corrections from a radiation bath can even temporarily erase the barrier. Using 122 three-dimensional stochastic Langevin lattice simulations in `CosmoLattice`—including Hubble expansion, spatial gradients, an evolving thermal bath, phenomenological friction $\eta = \gamma H$, and thermal noise—the authors test whether capturing the spatially averaged modulus guarantees that every region of space remains stabilized. They find that while the mean field closely tracks homogeneous evolution away from the capture threshold, near-critical trajectories linger near the unstable barrier top for roughly one e-fold, allowing tachyonic (negative-curvature) amplification of long-wavelength fluctuations to push localized patches over the barrier even as the spatial average turns back toward the vacuum. This demonstrates that standard homogeneous stabilization criteria are not sufficient to ensure global stabilization in a fluctuating early universe.

papers.title: Quantifying the Impact of Galactic Dark Matter Halo Models on LZ Results
papers.authors: Jialiang Shao, Andrea Addazi, Xinran Wang, Guanwen Fang, Yi-Fu Cai
papers.abstract: Most dark matter direct-detection limits are reported under the assumption of an isotropic, Maxwellian Standard Halo Model. However, the Milky Way's stellar halo exhibits substantial radial anisotropy, while cosmological simulations predict scale-dependent anisotropy in the dark matter velocity distribution. We investigate how departures from isotropy affect the interpretation of LZ results in two complementary regimes: background-dominated elastic-scattering searches and the recently reported 248 keV nuclear-recoil candidate, which we study using a background-free single-event approximation. For elastic scattering, we use the self-consistent isotropic, Osipkov-Merritt, axisymmetric, and triaxial halo models of Belli et al. and translate the published limits through the ratio of predicted event counts, applying a common escape-speed truncation in the Galactic frame. At WIMP masses above approximately 40 GeV, the resulting limits lie within about $\pm 30\%$ of the isotropic reference. Below approximately 15 GeV, the model envelope broadens to as much as an order of magnitude, reflecting sensitivity to the high-velocity tail. For the 248 keV event, the accessible inelastic mass splitting is likewise controlled by this tail. Some anisotropic models extend the allowed kinematic region towards splittings at which solar-neutrino constraints on a Higgsino interpretation become ineffective, although kinematic accessibility alone does not establish viability at the fixed Higgsino cross section. These results show that halo-model dependence is modest at high WIMP masses but becomes essential near kinematic thresholds.

conclusions: At high WIMP masses ($m_\chi \gtrsim 40\,\mathrm{GeV}$), halo-model choice has only a modest effect on LZ elastic spin-independent limits, keeping them within roughly $\pm 30\%$ ($R \approx 0.8\text{--}1.3$) of the isotropic Standard Halo Model, while varying the Galactic escape speed ($504\text{--}584\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$) shifts them by $\lesssim 5\%$.

Below $m_\chi \approx 15\,\mathrm{GeV}$, the model envelope broadens to up to an order of magnitude (e.g., $R \approx 0.17\text{--}1.63$ at $9\,\mathrm{GeV}$ for Osipkov–Merritt models), because lighter WIMPs require higher speeds to trigger an above-threshold recoil, making rates highly sensitive to the sparsely populated high-velocity tail.
Spin-dependent WIMP–nucleon limits follow the same qualitative halo-model pattern, though around $40\,\mathrm{GeV}$ nuclear-structure uncertainties exceed the halo-model variation.

For the $248\,\mathrm{keV}$ recoil candidate interpreted via endothermic inelastic scattering (e.g., a $\sim 1.1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ thermal Higgsino), the high-velocity tail controls the maximum accessible mass splitting $\delta$; some anisotropic models extend the kinematically allowed region toward splittings where solar-neutrino constraints weaken, though kinematic accessibility alone does not establish viability at the fixed Higgsino cross section.
ai.summary: Direct-detection experiments like the liquid-xenon LZ detector search for weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) scattering off atomic nuclei, and they typically report constraints assuming the Standard Halo Model (SHM)—a simple, isotropic Maxwellian velocity distribution for local Milky Way dark matter. Because both stellar-halo observations and cosmological simulations point to significant velocity anisotropy, the authors test how sensitive LZ's results are to more realistic halo models using 22 realizations from Belli et al. spanning isotropic spherical, Osipkov–Merritt anisotropic, axisymmetric (Evans), and triaxial Gaussian distributions. They rescale LZ's published spin-independent and spin-dependent elastic-scattering limits via predicted event-yield ratios with a common Galactic-frame escape-speed cutoff, and they also perform a background-free single-event analysis of LZ's recently reported $248\,\mathrm{keV}$ nuclear-recoil candidate under an endothermic inelastic-scattering scenario (where the WIMP upscatters to a slightly heavier state). The work demonstrates a clear hierarchy: astrophysical velocity-distribution assumptions are a minor systematic at high WIMP masses, but they become a dominant uncertainty near kinematic thresholds—such as low WIMP masses or high-energy inelastic recoils—where only the poorly constrained high-velocity tail can produce a signal.

papers.title: Pseudoscalar Yukawa Preheating via Effective Action Approach
papers.authors: Xi-Bin Li, De-Tian Zhao, Ke Fu, Jun-Yang Jiao
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate helicity-dependent fermion production driven by a pseudoscalar Yukawa interaction within the one-loop effective action framework. By integrating out the fermionic fields and employing the Schwinger proper time representation, we derive an analytical expression for the fermion pair production probability near each zero crossing of the oscillating inflaton field. We further introduce a helicity transfer matrix to describe the evolution of fermionic modes through successive non-adiabatic production events. For an undamped inflaton background, the temporal symmetry around successive zero crossings leads to the cancellation of helicity-mixing contributions after an even number of events, preventing the accumulation of helicity asymmetry. We then extend the analysis to a damped oscillatory background, in which the decreasing inflaton amplitude breaks this temporal symmetry and modifies the transfer matrix at each crossing. The resulting non-commuting transfer matrices produce a persistent helical spectrum, as demonstrated by the probabilities as a function of momentum obtained after successive scattering events. A comparison with scalar Yukawa preheating further confirms the role of helicity mixing in generating the helical asymmetry induced by pseudoscalar mechanism. These results establish an effective action framework for studying helicity asymmetry during fermionic preheating and provide insight into the influence of the inflaton's dynamical evolution on particle production.

conclusions: Near each zero crossing of the oscillating inflaton, the mode equation reduces to an inverted harmonic oscillator, yielding an analytical single-crossing pair-production probability suppressed exponentially in $(k^2 + m_\psi^2) / (g\phi_0 m_\phi)$.

For an undamped inflaton background, time-reflection symmetry across successive zero crossings causes off-diagonal helicity-mixing terms to cancel after every even number of crossings, preventing any lasting helicity asymmetry.

When realistic damping of the inflaton amplitude is included, this symmetry is broken and the crossing-dependent transfer matrices no longer commute; numerical evaluation across $N = 1, 3, 5, 8, 25, 40$ oscillations shows a persistent net helical asymmetry that increasingly concentrates at low momenta (the infrared) as the resonance window narrows.

Comparing with standard scalar Yukawa preheating confirms that pseudoscalar helicity mixing drives the asymmetry, and the authors explicitly connect their effective-action transfer matrix $\exp\mathbf{T}$ to the standard Bogoliubov-coefficient formalism.
ai.summary: After cosmic inflation ends, the oscillating inflaton field can explosively produce particles through non-perturbative bursts known as *preheating*, which occur each time the inflaton passes through zero. When the inflaton couples to Dirac fermions via a pseudoscalar (axion-like) Yukawa interaction ($-g\phi\bar{\psi}\mathrm{i}\gamma^5\psi$), this process can generate a *helicity asymmetry*—an imbalance between left- and right-handed fermions that is of interest for early-universe baryogenesis and primordial magnetic fields. Rather than solving mode equations directly with Bogoliubov transformations, the authors integrate out the fermions to compute the one-loop effective action using the Schwinger proper-time method, and introduce a *helicity transfer matrix* to track how fermionic modes evolve across successive zero crossings. They show that while an idealized, undamped inflaton cannot build up a lasting asymmetry due to symmetry cancellations, realistic damping of the inflaton amplitude breaks this symmetry and produces a persistent helical fermion spectrum.

papers.title: Reliability of Fermi/GBM spectral-catalogue parameters for gamma-ray burst population studies
papers.authors: Istvan Horvath
papers.abstract: The Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) spectral catalogue contains measurements affected by model uncertainties, different peak-flux (PFLX) integration times, and changes in catalogue processing. We examine which quantities describe spectral shape and which reflect brightness or measurement conditions. We analysed 3337 of 3378 GRBs with spectral-fit data and identified a catalogue transition at GRB180712358. We compared the two periods using rank-based tests, regressions, and catalogue model-selection rules, and assessed duration classification by repeated cross-validation. PFLX measurements at 64 and nominal 1024 ms were analysed separately; short-long comparisons used fluence (FLNC) measurements only. The transition coincides with changes in catalogue version, fit statistic, and fit fields. In the nominal 1024 ms sample, all ten COMP A-B rank-biserial effects have absolute values below 0.10. In the 64 ms sample, COMP shape parameters are similar, but amplitudes, fluxes, and fluences are higher in the later period. The origin of this difference is unknown. In the earlier period, brighter bursts have smaller parameter errors but larger reported fit statistics and stronger evidence for spectral curvature. The FLNC PLAW index measures broad-band hardness. BAND alpha and Epeak can describe spectral shape when their errors are controlled, but beta is often poorly constrained. Adding PLAW or BAND to COMP provides little additional duration-classification information in matched samples. We interpret the A-B division mainly as a catalogue-processing transition, not population evolution. Fit statistics, errors, metadata, and model labels describe measurement conditions and should not be treated as independent physical variables. Correlated model parameters should not be treated as independent.

conclusions: A sharp transition occurs at GRB180712358 (July 2018), where the catalogue version, fit statistic (Castor C-STAT to PSTAT), and reported reduced fit statistics all jump simultaneously; this reflects a processing change rather than astrophysical population evolution.

Peak-flux (PFLX) spectra use 64 ms windows for short bursts and 1024 ms windows for long bursts (a factor of 16 difference), so they must be compared only within fixed time scales, while short–long physical comparisons should rely on time-integrated fluence (FLNC) measurements.

Across the pre- and post-transition periods, COMP spectral-shape parameters remain stable: in the 1024 ms sample all ten physical rank-biserial effect sizes are small ($|r_{\rm rb}| < 0.10$), whereas in the 64 ms sample amplitudes, fluxes, and fluences are systematically higher in the later period ($r_{\rm rb} = 0.241\text{--}0.289$), likely partly due to sample selection.

In the earlier catalogue period, brighter bursts show smaller formal parameter errors but larger reported fit statistics and stronger evidence for spectral curvature, demonstrating that parameter precision and goodness-of-fit track different things.

The FLNC power-law index is a reliable broad-band hardness proxy, and BAND $\alpha$ and $E_{\rm peak}$ are usable when their errors are controlled (whereas the high-energy index $\beta$ is often poorly constrained); however, adding PLAW or BAND to a well-measured COMP fit adds little duration-classification power, and fit statistics, errors, and metadata should never be treated as independent physical variables.
ai.summary: Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are commonly sorted into short and long classes by duration, but efforts to identify finer physical subclasses using multivariate clustering of catalogue data are easily misled by brightness biases, correlated model parameters, and instrument-processing artifacts. In this paper, Horvath audits 3337 GRBs from the Fermi Gamma-ray Burst Monitor (GBM) spectral catalogue—which fits prompt-emission spectra over both the full burst (fluence, FLNC) and the brightest interval (peak flux, PFLX) using empirical models like a power law (PLAW), a cutoff power law (COMP), and the broken-power-law BAND function—to separate genuine spectral-shape indicators from measurement conditions. Using rank-based statistical comparisons, regressions, and cross-validated duration classification, the author identifies a sharp catalogue-processing transition in July 2018 and shows how different PFLX integration windows (64 ms vs. 1024 ms) and brightness-dependent fit statistics distort naive comparisons. The study establishes strict variable-selection rules so that future GRB population and clustering analyses do not mistake catalogue artifacts or brightness subdivisions for distinct astrophysical classes.

papers.title: Superheavy gravitational dark matter from runaway bubble collisions
papers.authors: Cheng-Wei Chiang, Van Que Tran
papers.abstract: A stable particle that couples only through gravity is pair-produced in collisions of runaway bubble walls by graviton exchange. For a transition of duration $1/\beta$, a Dirac fermion reaches the yield $Y_X\simeq6.8\times10^{-3}(H/\beta)(T_{\rm reh}/M_{\rm P})^3$, where $H$ is the Hubble rate of the vacuum energy, $T_{\rm reh}$ the reheating temperature and $M_{\rm P}$ the reduced Planck mass. The yield is flat up to masses near $(H/\beta)M_{\rm P}/\nu^2$, where $\nu$ of order one sets the wall-field excursion. Gravity alone then gives dark matter up to about $10^{17}$~GeV at reheating temperatures far below its mass, where freeze-in fails.

conclusions: For a Dirac fermion DM particle, first collisions of runaway walls produce a yield $Y_X \simeq 6.8 \times 10^{-3} (H/\beta)(T_{\rm reh}/M_{\rm P})^3$ that is flat in $M_X$ up to the collision scale $\bar{M}_{\rm coll} \simeq 11 (H/\beta) M_{\rm P}/\nu^2$ (with cosmic expansion reducing it by $\approx e^{-4H/\beta}$), independent of the detailed wall profile.

$1+1$D nonlinear lattice simulations of relativistic kink–antikink collisions ($\gamma = 80, 160$) confirm that the walls pass cleanly through each other where heavy pairs form, matching the analytic parton prediction to the percent level.

Purely gravitational production from runaway transitions can explain the full observed DM abundance ($\Omega_X h^2 = 0.12$) for superheavy masses $M_X \sim 10^{10}\text{–}3\times 10^{17}$ GeV at reheating temperatures up to six orders of magnitude below $M_X$, where thermal freeze-in fails and (for $M_X > H_{\rm inf}$) inflationary production is suppressed.

Because gravity couples universally, the first-collision yield sets a robust lower bound on the abundance of any stable, purely gravitational particle in a runaway transition (and thus an upper bound on $T_{\rm reh}$ to avoid overproducing DM).

The same bubble collisions emit high-frequency gravitational waves peaking at $10^4\text{–}10^7$ Hz—above current and planned detector bands, though the strongest realizations reach above the quantum limit for dedicated high-frequency interferometers around $3\times 10^4\text{–}5\times 10^5$ Hz.
ai.summary: If dark matter (DM) interacts with ordinary matter only through gravity, producing very heavy DM in the early universe is difficult: thermal freeze-in (graviton-mediated scattering in the primordial plasma) is exponentially suppressed for masses above the reheating temperature $T_{\rm reh}$, and gravitational production at the end of inflation is capped by the inflationary Hubble rate $H_{\rm inf}$. This paper studies a much more energetic gravitational channel: first-order phase transitions in which bubbles of true vacuum expand with negligible plasma friction, so their walls accelerate continuously ("run away") to ultra-relativistic speeds and collide at energies far exceeding $T_{\rm reh}$. The authors calculate DM pair production via $s$-channel graviton exchange between colliding walls using both a parton (wall-field quanta) description and a classical-source approach, validate their free-passage assumption with $1+1$D nonlinear lattice simulations of wall collisions, and sum exactly over oblique angles and bubble-size distributions for exponential nucleation (plus cosmological Monte Carlo checks for an expanding background). They show that this universal mechanism produces a flat yield up to near-Planckian masses, opening a viable window for superheavy gravitational DM up to $\sim 10^{17}$ GeV at low reheating temperatures while also setting a model-independent lower bound on the abundance of any stable particle in such a transition.

papers.title: Exact analytic solutions for the $n=1$ chameleon field in planar systems with an arbitrary number of uniform layers
papers.authors: Chad Briddon, Mario Pitschmann
papers.abstract: Scalar fields have long been investigated as a potential dark energy candidate. Of these models, screened scalar fields like the chameleon have received interest due to their ability to avoid observational constraints. However, the non-linear nature of these models has led to there being only a small number of exact analytic solutions within the literature. In this work, we present exact analytic solutions for the $n=1$ chameleon model in a planar system consisting of $N$ discrete regions of uniform density. We compare these to the relevant approximate solutions within the literature. We also use our solutions to forecast constraints from CANNEX, a recent experiment devised to measure Casimir forces and detect hypothetical fifth forces. Unlike in previous works, we consider the full fifteen-layered setup of CANNEX, as opposed to treating the plate and wall as single uniform objects. Doing so revealed an increase in the induced chameleon pressure of up to $\sim 7 \%$. However, the resulting gain is insufficient to probe new regions of parameter space at the projected sensitivities.

conclusions: Derived exact analytic field profiles (expressed in terms of Jacobi elliptic functions) for the $n=1$ chameleon model across $N$ planar layers of arbitrary thickness and uniform density, covering all three interior regimes (profiles with a maximum, a minimum, or crossing the local expectation value).

Validated the exact solutions against existing approximate planar solutions in the literature and identified mathematical errors in a previously published exact two-plate solution with non-zero vacuum density (showing it only holds as an approximation when the peak field is far below its vacuum expectation value).

Applied the $N$-layer formalism to the full 15-layer geometry of the CANNEX parallel-plate experiment, finding that accounting for the realistic multi-layer plate structure increases the predicted chameleon-induced pressure by up to $\sim 7\%$ compared to simplified uniform-plate approximations.

Showed that this $\sim 7\%$ pressure boost is too small to open up new regions of chameleon parameter space at CANNEX's projected sensitivities, though the publicly released Python package provides a rigorous tool for forecasting future laboratory fifth-force experiments.
ai.relevance_reason: Although the chameleon mechanism is a key screening model in modified gravity, this paper focuses strictly on 1D analytic solutions for laboratory fifth-force experiments rather than cosmological N-body simulations, emulators, or large-scale structure observables.
ai.summary: Chameleon models are a popular class of screened scalar-field dark energy and modified gravity theories in which the field's effective mass increases with local matter density, hiding any associated "fifth force" in dense environments like the Solar System while leaving it active on cosmological scales. Because the chameleon equation of motion is strongly non-linear, laboratory tests—such as parallel-plate Casimir/fifth-force experiments (CANNEX), bouncing ultracold neutrons (qBOUNCE), and torsion balances (Eöt-Wash)—have historically relied on approximate or idealized two-layer analytic profiles that ignore realistic multi-layer plate compositions or non-zero vacuum densities. In this paper, Briddon and Pitschmann derive exact 1D analytic solutions for the static $n=1$ chameleon field across an arbitrary number $N$ of uniform planar layers using Jacobi elliptic functions, matching the field continuously across all interfaces and assuming only that the outermost layers are effectively infinite compared to the local Compton wavelength. They also release a Python package implementing these solutions and apply it to the full 15-layer experimental setup of CANNEX to test how much realistic plate layering affects fifth-force forecasts.

papers.title: Analytic $k$-essence Inflation
papers.authors: V.K. Oikonomou
papers.abstract: In this work we develop a fully analytic $k$-essence inflation solution which is compatible with the observational constraints on inflation, without the need for the slow-roll assumption being imposed dynamically in the field equations. The analytic solution is obtained for a kinetic scalar sector of the form $K(X)= \frac{X^n}{X_s^{n-1}}$ and for the scalar field satisfying a tracking condition $\dot{\phi}^2=\gamma H^{-m}$. For this class of theories, the sound speed of the primordial curvature perturbations is constant, so no gradient instabilities occur in the theory. The Hubble rate, the scale factor and the scalar field can be analytically expressed as functions of the cosmic time, and the observational indices of inflation depend solely on the parameters $n$ and $m$. The resulting evolution is inflationary and it develops a pressure singularity a few $e$-foldings after the end of inflation. However, using qualitative and quantitative numerical arguments, we show that the pressure singularity is classically avoided when the matter fluids of radiation and cold dark matter are taken into account.

conclusions: The model yields closed-form expressions for $H(t)$, $\phi(t)$, and the inflationary observables solely in terms of $(m, n)$ and the $e$-folding number $N_*$, with a constant perturbation sound speed $c_A^2 = (2n-1)^{-1}$ that avoids gradient instabilities for $n > 1/2$.

For the fiducial choice $(m, n) = (2, 3)$ and $N_* = 50\text{--}55$, the model predicts $n_s \simeq 0.975\text{--}0.977$, $r \simeq 0.016\text{--}0.018$, and running $\alpha_s \simeq -(4\text{--}5)\times 10^{-4}$, fitting comfortably within recent ACT ($n_s = 0.9743 \pm 0.0034$) and Planck/BICEP ($r < 0.036$) bounds.
Although slow-roll is not imposed by hand in the field equations, the tracking condition automatically induces a slow-roll regime during inflation ($\rho_{\rm kin}/V \propto \epsilon_1 \ll 1$).

In pure vacuum, the solution hits a Type II pressure singularity $N_{\rm post} = (mn+2)^{-1}$ ($0.125$ $e$-folds for the fiducial model) after inflation ends, but numerical integration with radiation and CDM shows the tracking condition breaks in the final $\sim 0.05$ $e$-folds and the singularity is smoothly avoided.
ai.summary: Recent CMB data from ACT favor a slightly less red-tilted primordial power spectrum than Planck alone, putting pressure on many standard single-field inflation models. To address this without modifying General Relativity, the author constructs a fully analytic $k$-essence inflation model—a scalar-field theory with a non-standard kinetic term $K(X) = X^n / X_s^{n-1}$—by imposing a "tracking" relation $\dot{\phi}^2 = \gamma H^{-m}$ between the field's velocity and the Hubble rate. This ansatz allows the Friedmann and Raychaudhuri equations to be solved in closed form, fixing the scalar potential and expressing the spectral index $n_s$, tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$, and running $\alpha_s$ purely in terms of two parameters $(m, n)$ and the number of $e$-folds $N_*$. While the pure scalar-field solution hits a finite-time "pressure singularity" (where the effective pressure diverges even though the scale factor and energy density remain finite) shortly after inflation ends, numerical integrations show that adding classical radiation and dark matter fluids disrupts the tracking condition just in time to avoid the singularity smoothly.

papers.title: The Sensitivity of Gamma-Ray Searches for Dark Matter Annihilation in Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies: the LSST Era and Beyond
papers.authors: Ilumi Chavez, Aditya Ghosh, Chris Kelso, Dan Hooper, Alex Drlica-Wagner, Ethan O. Nadler
papers.abstract: We forecast the sensitivity of gamma-ray searches to dark matter annihilation in Milky Way satellite dwarf galaxies using BabyBison, a Monte Carlo pipeline combining cosmological satellite simulations and observational selection functions with a joint likelihood analysis of gamma-ray data. Although LSST is expected to substantially expand the catalog of known satellite galaxies, we find that these discoveries are likely to produce only modest improvements in the resulting dark matter annihilation constraints, typically below 20\%. Much more substantial gains are possible, however, in relatively rare realizations that contain yet-to-be-discovered satellites with large $J$-factors. These results reinforce the fact that indirect detection analyses using the population of dwarf galaxies are typically driven in large part by a small number of high-$J$-factor systems rather than by the total satellite count. We present projections for the sensitivity of Fermi-LAT and the proposed Advanced Particle-astrophysics Telescope (APT) to dark matter annihilation, finding that a complete census of the Milky Way dwarf sample could enable such instruments to probe dark matter with masses up to the TeV scale. We also investigate the dark matter discovery potential of these instruments and project their ability to measure the properties of an annihilating dark matter particle.

conclusions: LSST is projected to discover a median of $66^{+20}_{-16}$ (SMW) or $45^{+16}_{-11}$ (MWest) new Milky Way dwarf galaxies, yet in typical realizations this improves stacked gamma-ray upper limits on the dark matter annihilation cross section $\langle\sigma v\rangle$ by less than 20%.

Stacked indirect-detection constraints are dominated by a handful of nearby, high-$J$-factor systems rather than total satellite count, so much larger sensitivity gains occur only in rare realizations where LSST finds an unusually high-$J$ dwarf.

A complete "ultimate" census of Milky Way satellites—including faint, compact systems ($M_V > 0$, $r_{1/2} < 10\,\mathrm{pc}$) excluded from the baseline LSST sample—shifts the highest expected $J$-factors from $\log_{10}[J/(\mathrm{GeV^2\,cm^{-5}})] \sim 19.8$ to $\sim 20.5$, allowing Fermi-LAT to test thermal-relic dark matter up to several hundred GeV and the proposed APT to reach the TeV scale.

For a benchmark dark matter signal motivated by the Galactic Center gamma-ray excess, LSST discoveries modestly increase detection odds and parameter precision, whereas a complete satellite census would substantially improve measurements of the dark matter mass $m_\chi$ and $\langle\sigma v\rangle$.
ai.summary: Indirect dark matter searches look for gamma rays produced when weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) annihilate in dense, dark-matter-dominated systems like Milky Way satellite dwarf galaxies, which have very little competing astrophysical gamma-ray emission. The expected signal from each dwarf scales with its $J$-factor—the line-of-sight integral of the squared dark matter density—and combining many dwarfs in a joint likelihood strengthens constraints on the annihilation cross section $\langle\sigma v\rangle$. To forecast how upcoming optical surveys will impact these searches, the authors introduce BabyBison, a Monte Carlo pipeline that combines Milky Way-like dark-matter-only zoom-in simulations (SymphonyMilkyWay and MilkyWay-est), an empirical galaxy–halo connection model, and survey selection functions to simulate gamma-ray observations with Fermi-LAT and the proposed Advanced Particle-astrophysics Telescope (APT). They find that although the Rubin Observatory's LSST will discover dozens of new Milky Way satellites, typical realizations yield only modest (<20%) improvements in annihilation constraints because the limits are driven by just a few high-$J$-factor systems. Achieving much stronger gains—potentially probing thermal-relic dark matter up to the TeV scale and testing dark matter interpretations of the Galactic Center gamma-ray excess—will require either discovering rare high-$J$ dwarfs or completing a census of fainter, more compact satellites.

papers.title: JAISP: A Joint Rubin-Euclid Foundation Model for Cross-Instrument Source Detection and Astrometry
papers.authors: Shoubaneh Hemmati, George Helou, Yu-Heng Lin, Rachel Akeson, Charles Darren Dowell, Andreas Faisst, Thomas Greene, David Shupe
papers.abstract: Joint pixel-level processing of Rubin and Euclid imaging promises deeper source detection and the cross-survey consistency that precision cosmology requires. We introduce JAISP (Joint AI Survey Processing), a foundation model that learns a single representation of ten-band imaging: Rubin ugrizy and Euclid VIS, Y, J, and H, from the first public releases over $\approx 0.2$ deg$^2$ of the ECDFS deep field. Trained without labels by predicting each band from the other nine, its frozen encoder drives small task-specific networks for source detection and astrometry. The detection network recovers nearly all VIS-selected Euclid Q1 catalog sources on held-out sky, and source injection shows that combining all ten bands extends the point-source detection limit by $\approx 0.3$ mag beyond VIS alone. The astrometry network transfers the sharp VIS localization to the other nine bands, reducing median cross-band positional offsets from $\approx 50$ to $6$--$10$ mas while retaining the full precision of its VIS centroid anchor even for faint sources. Separating this per-source scatter exposes the cross-survey concordance field: a coherent $9$--$10$ mas offset between the two independently Gaia-registered astrometric solutions, dominated by a component common to all bands. Applied without retraining to a second Euclid Deep Field, both networks perform without measurable loss. These gains serve the joint-survey science case: a deeper census recovers faint neighbors whose blending biases weak-lensing shapes and photometric redshifts, and VIS-grade positions in every band supply the common astrometric reference that joint photometry and faint-source proper motions require. A single representation learned once from survey pixels thus serves several measurements across the sky.

conclusions: **Deeper joint source detection:** Combining all ten Rubin + Euclid bands extends the 50% point-source detection limit by $\approx 0.3$ mag beyond Euclid VIS alone (reaching VIS $\approx 26.7$ for point sources and $25.2$ for moderately extended galaxies), adding $\sim 20\%$ more faint sources and helping identify faint blended neighbors that would otherwise bias weak-lensing shapes and photo-$z$'s.

**VIS-grade astrometry across all bands:** The astrometry head transfers Euclid VIS's sharp localization to the coarser Rubin and NISP bands, shrinking median cross-band positional offsets from $\sim 45$–$50$ mas down to $6$–$10$ mas and achieving $\sim 17$ mas accuracy at $\mathrm{S/N}=5$ (nearly matching the $\sim 16$ mas VIS centroid anchor).

**Exposing cross-survey systematics:** Removing per-source scatter reveals a coherent $9$–$10$ mas "concordance field" offset between Rubin's and Euclid's independently Gaia-calibrated astrometric frames—dominated by a $\sim 7$ mas shift common to all bands rather than band-specific errors.

**Zero-shot transfer and low compute cost:** Pretraining takes only $\sim 8$ GPU-hours on a single L40S GPU (with lightweight $<1$M-parameter task heads), and both networks transfer without retraining or measurable loss to a completely separate sky region (Euclid Deep Field South).
ai.relevance_reason: While this paper uses Euclid Q1 data and addresses observational systematics (blending and astrometry) relevant to Euclid weak lensing, it is a pure pixel-level image-processing and machine-learning instrumentation paper rather than non-linear theory, simulations, or emulators for beyond-$\Lambda$CDM cosmology.
ai.summary: Precision cosmology with upcoming overlapping surveys like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory (LSST) and ESA's Euclid mission is increasingly limited by observational systematics—especially galaxy blending in ground-based images and tiny positional mismatches (astrometric scatter) between instruments that bias weak-lensing shapes and photometric redshifts. To tackle this at the pixel level, the authors introduce JAISP (Joint AI Survey Processing), a ~9.1M-parameter self-supervised foundation model trained on ten-band imaging (Rubin $ugrizy$ plus Euclid VIS and near-infrared $YJH$) over $\approx 0.2\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ of the ECDFS deep field from the first public releases (Rubin DP1 and Euclid Q1). Rather than using contrastive or embedding-alignment objectives—which they show fail to preserve sub-pixel source positions—they train a two-stream ConvNeXt + transformer encoder to reconstruct one withheld wavelength band from the other nine, then freeze the encoder to drive lightweight task heads for source detection and astrometry. This single learned representation transfers Euclid VIS's sharp space-based localization to all ten bands, deepens faint-source detection, and generalizes without retraining to a separate Euclid deep field, demonstrating a much cheaper, reusable alternative to building monolithic classical joint-processing pipelines from scratch.

papers.title: Primordial B-mode sensitivity forecasts for northern-sky cosmic microwave background surveys
papers.authors: Dongdong Zhang, Bo Wang, Jia-Rui Li, Yi-Fu Cai, Chang Feng
papers.abstract: Northern-sky cosmic microwave background (CMB) polarization observations offer additional sky coverage and independent measurements in the search for primordial gravitational waves. We assess their potential through idealized sensitivity forecasts motivated by the Ali CMB Polarization Telescope. Using a power-spectrum likelihood and Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, we relate assumed map depths, accessible angular scales, and effective sky coverage to constraints on the tensor-to-scalar ratio $r$. The model retains lensing B modes and assumes negligible residual foreground power. A benchmark with 95 and 150\,GHz channels, a polarization map depth of $40\,\mu\mathrm{K\,arcmin}$ per channel, and $f_{\rm sky}=0.1$ yields $\sigma(r)=0.023$ for a fiducial $r=0.014$, improving to 0.015 with Planck-like mock data. At a per-channel depth of $10\,\mu\mathrm{K\,arcmin}$, the northern survey alone reaches $\sigma(r)=0.0031$. Raising the minimum multipole from 30 to 70 degrades the baseline sensitivity to 0.037, while extending the effective area at fixed depth improves the constraint. As the northern maps deepen, their contribution increasingly determines the precision on $r$, whereas Planck-like information continues to constrain the scalar spectral index. These forecasts quantify the scope for improved northern-sky tensor constraints and establish sensitivity benchmarks for subsequent studies of joint northern and southern CMB observations.

papers.title: Quantum cosmological perturbations in bouncing models with mimetic dark matter
papers.authors: Idaiane L. Machado, Dêivid R. da Silva, Nelson Pinto-Neto
papers.abstract: We calculate the power spectrum of cosmological perturbations originated from quantum vacuum fluctuations in bouncing scenarios proposed in Ref.~\cite{chamseddine2014cosmology} in the framework of mimetic cosmology. We show that all physically relevant models produce scale-invariant spectral indices and amplitudes compatible with observations, provided that the bounce occurs at length scales $t_0$ inside the physically reasonable interval $10^5 l_p < t_0 < 10^9 l_p$. We also show that by slightly modifying the scalar field potential proposed in Ref.~\cite{chamseddine2014cosmology}, we can obtain the observed red-tilted spectral index, with the same amplitude constraints. The underlying theory contains instability problems yet to be solved. However, the methods we constructed and the results we obtained may be sufficiently general to be applied to the infrared limit of some yet to be constructed healthy mimetic cosmology, providing reasonable bouncing cosmological models without the need for any background quantum effect.

papers.title: CMB constraints on $U(1)$ axion warm inflation
papers.authors: Asma Alaei, Sukannya Bhattacharya, Vahid Kamali
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose a model of warm inflation driven by axion-like particles interacting with $U(1)$ gauge fields, with implications for the early universe's thermal evolution. By extending traditional warm inflation models, we introduce a dissipation mechanism through the thermal fluctuations of electromagnetic fields, leading to a non-trivial back-reaction on the inflaton's dynamics. Our results are consistent with CMB observations, even for a natural sub-Plankian Axion decay constant $f\leq M_{\rm Pl}$. We present precise constraints on the model's free parameters, using CAMB and CosmoMC codes. These findings offer new insights into the thermal history of the universe and the nature of inflationary dynamics.

papers.title: Rapid late-time reionization: constraints and cosmological implications
papers.authors: Willem Elbers
papers.abstract: We present constraints on the reionization optical depth, $\tau$, obtained using several independent methods. First, we perform a non-parametric reconstruction of the reionization history, using Lyman-$\alpha$ constraints on the evolution of the volume-averaged neutral hydrogen fraction, $x_\mathrm{HI}(z)$, including recent results from JWST. When combined with BAO measurements from DESI and BBN constraints, these data imply a rapid reionization history ($z_\mathrm{mid}=6.99^{+0.12}_{-0.18}$ and $\Delta z_{50}=1.09^{+0.10}_{-0.28}$) and a value of $\tau=0.0491^{+0.0014}_{-0.0031}$, which is largely insensitive to the assumed cosmological model and independent of CMB data. The optical depth can also be measured from large-scale $(\ell<30)$ CMB polarization data, yielding constraints that are similarly model-insensitive and consistent with the Ly$\alpha$ bound. Third, $\tau$ may be constrained from the attenuation of small-scale $(\ell>30)$ CMB anisotropies, but the results are sensitive to the choice of cosmological model. Assuming $\Lambda$CDM and combining small-scale CMB data with CMB lensing and type 1a supernovae (SNe) yields tight constraints that are compatible with the Ly$\alpha$ bound. Adding galaxy clustering and lensing measurements brings the constraints further into agreement with the Ly$\alpha$ bound. These independent results reinforce a consensus picture in which reionization is rapid and late. However, the combination of small-scale CMB, CMB lensing, and BAO data yields $\tau=0.094\pm0.011$, which is in $4\sigma$ tension with our Ly$\alpha$ bound. Non-standard reionization scenarios, or relaxing our assumption that the onset of reionization occurs after $z=15$, can reconcile some but not all constraints. Concordance is restored in alternative cosmological models, such as models with dynamical dark energy favoured by BAO, CMB, and SNe data.

papers.title: Solving the Domain Wall Problem: Primordial Magnetic Fields as a Dynamical Solution
papers.authors: Zizhuo Zhao, Yuefeng Di, Ligong Bian, Jing Shu
papers.abstract: To prevent overclosing the Universe, stable domain walls must decay-a problem typically addressed by breaking the Peccei-Quinn symmetry with a bias term. In this Letter, we present a novel mechanism in which a helical primordial magnetic field provides a spatially inhomogeneous Chern-Simons source that drives the axion field. We validate this mechanism through three-dimensional lattice simulations of the evolving domain-wall network, demonstrating its efficacy in inducing decay. Our quantitative analysis reveals that the correlation length of the primordial magnetic field is a crucial determinant of the decay rate of the network and the properties of the emitted axions and gravitational waves. In particular, the axion emitted from the decaying domain-wall network can contribute to the dark matter abundance, and the associated gravitational-wave signal lies in the frequency range probed by pulsar timing array experiments.

papers.title: Observational constraints on early time non-phantom behaviour of dynamical dark energy
papers.authors: Sk. Sohail, Sonej Alam, Md. Wali Hossain
papers.abstract: We investigate dynamical dark energy models in which the scalar field component is non-phantom at early times. The models include a single-exponential thawing field, a double-exponential scaling--thawing field, and extensions in which a steep exponential scaling field is combined with a cosmological constant, a constant-$w$ fluid, or a CPL fluid. We confront them with Planck PR4 CMB temperature, polarisation and lensing data, DESI DR2 BAO measurements and the Pantheon$+$ supernova sample. The background parameters are stable across all models, with $H_0 \simeq 67.7$--$68.3\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, so none of the models relieves the Hubble tension. The CPL parametrization prefers $w_0>-1$ and $w_a<0$ at $\sim\!2.7\sigma$ relative to $\Lambda$CDM, corresponding to phantom behaviour at low redshift. The constant-$w$ and thawing models remain consistent with a cosmological constant. When an early scaling phase is added, the data limit the peak early dark energy fraction to $f_{\mathrm{EDE}}<0.0075$ ($f_{\mathrm{EDE}}<0.015$ for SC$+$CPL). This requires a steep potential, $\lambda_2 \gtrsim 30$, and keeps the scalar-field density below the half-percent level at matter--radiation equality. Early scaling dynamics therefore cannot alter the sound horizon enough to address the Hubble tension. The scaling models fit the data as well as $\Lambda$CDM ($\Delta\chi^2_{\mathrm{min}}\lesssim 1.4$), but they are disfavoured by AIC and BIC because of their additional, weakly constrained parameters. Adding a scaling field to CPL does not improve the fit. Late-time evolving dark energy is mildly preferred by the data, while a simple early scaling phase offers no benefit.

papers.title: A single field inflationary model consistent with recent observations: reheating and radiative stability
papers.authors: Md. Wali Hossain
papers.abstract: We study single field inflation with the inverse exponential potential, which has one free parameter besides the energy scale. For a wide range of parameter space, its predictions for the scalar spectral index and the tensor to scalar ratio lie within the $1\sigma$ region of the combined SPA$+$BK$+$DESI data, and the wider family of inverse power law exponential potentials behaves similarly. We compare these predictions with those of the $R^2$ model, monomial potentials, $\alpha$-attractors, non-minimally coupled Higgs like inflation and a radiatively corrected plateau potential. The $R^2$ and monomial predictions lie near or outside the $2\sigma$ boundary of the same data, whereas the non-minimally coupled Higgs like and radiatively corrected plateau families overlap the favoured contours over part of their parameter space. To describe reheating, we add a steep exponential term that is negligible during inflation and, together with the inverse exponential term, creates a minimum about which the inflaton oscillates. The maximum reheating temperatures are $T_{\rm rh}\sim10^{12}$--$10^{13}\,{\rm GeV}$, consistent with the Big Bang Nucleosynthesis bound. Coupling the inflaton to a Dirac fermion through a Yukawa interaction, these temperatures require couplings comparable to the standard model charged lepton Yukawa couplings. Nonperturbative fermion production transfers negligible energy, and perturbative decay completes reheating. The same coupling induces a one loop correction to the inflationary potential, which limits the radiatively safe reheating temperature to $T_{\rm rh}\lesssim10^{12}\,{\rm GeV}$.

papers.title: The Impact of Galaxy Formation on Galaxy Biasing, and Implications for Primordial non-Gaussianity Constraints
papers.authors: Lucia A. Perez, Shy Genel, Elisabeth Krause, Rachel S. Somerville
papers.abstract: The parameter $f_{\textrm{NL}}$ measures the local non-Gaussianity in the primordial energy fluctuations of the Universe, with any deviation from $f_{\textrm{NL}}=0$ providing key constraints on inflationary models. Galaxy clustering is sensitive to $f_{\textrm{NL}}$ at large scale modes and the next generation of galaxy surveys will approach a statistical error of $\sigma_{f_{\textrm{NL}}}\sim1$. However, the systematic errors on these constraints are dominated by the degeneracy of $f_{\textrm{NL}}$ with the galaxy bias parameters $b_1$ (galaxy overdensities caused by mass perturbations) and $b_{\phi}$ (galaxy overdensities caused by primordial potential perturbations). It has been shown that the assumed scaling of $b_{\phi}(z)=2\delta_c (b_1(z)-1)$ is not accurate for realistically simulated galaxies, and depends both on the galaxy selection and the way that galaxies are modeled. To address this, we leverage the CAMELS-SAM pipeline to explore how varying parameters of galaxy formation affects $b_{\phi}$ and $b_1$ for various galaxy selections. We run separate-universe N-body simulations of $L=205 h^{-1}$ cMpc and $N=1280^3$ to measure $b_{\phi}$, and run 55 unique instances of the Santa Cruz semi-analytic model with varying parameters of stellar and AGN feedback. We find the behavior and evolution of a SC-SAM model's stellar-, SFR- and sSFR- to halo mass relationships track well with how $b_1$ and $b_{\phi}(b_1)$ change across redshift and selection for the SC-SAM. We find our variations of the SC-SAM encapsulate the $b_{\phi}$ behavior previously measured in IllustrisTNG, the Munich SAM, and this http URL , we identify sSFR selections as particularly robust to varied galaxy modeling.

papers.authors: DES Collaboration : T. M. C. Abbott, M. Aguena, A. Alarcon, O. Alves, A. Amon, D. Anbajagane, F. Andrade-Oliveira, W. d'Assignies, S. Avila, D. Bacon, J. Beas-Gonzalez, K. Bechtol, M.
